source.author: stat
source.text: Ecce autem hortatus Eteoclis et arma secuti, lecta manus, iuvenes, quos nec Tritonia bello, nec prope collata sprevisset cuspide Mavors, adventant; contra collecta ut pectora parmae fixerat atque hastam longe protenderat, haeret arduus Hippomedon: ceu fluctibus obvia rupes, cui neque de caelo metus et fracta aequora cedunt, stat cunctis immota minis, fugit ipse rigentem pontus et ex alto miserae novere carinae.
source.text_original: Ecce autem hortatus Eteoclis et arma secuti, / lecta manus, iuvenes, quos nec Tritonia bello, / nec prope collata sprevisset cuspide Mavors, / adventant; contra collecta ut pectora parmae / fixerat atque hastam longe protenderat, haeret / arduus Hippomedon: ceu fluctibus obvia rupes, / cui neque de caelo metus et fracta aequora cedunt, / stat cunctis immota minis, fugit ipse rigentem / pontus et ex alto miserae novere carinae.
source.text_english: But behold, having taken up Eteocles’ exhortation and arms, a chosen band of young men, whom neither Tritonia in war nor Mavors with spear drawn near would have despised, are approaching; against them Hippomedon stands towering, having planted his shield against his gathered breast and thrust his spear far out: like a rock facing the waves, from which neither fear from the sky nor the shattered sea withdraws, it stands unmoved amid all threats; the sea itself flees the stiff rock, and the wretched keels have come to know it from the deep.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: quin etiam Herculeo consurgit ab ordine Tydeus Nelidesque Periclymenus, quem parva Methone felevis Elis equis et fluctibus obvius Aulon caestibus adversos viderunt frangere vultus. Tu quoque Phrixeos remo, Poeantie, Colchos bis Lemnon visure petis, nunc cuspide patris inclitus, Herculeas olim moture sagittas.
reuse.text_original: quin etiam Herculeo consurgit ab ordine Tydeus / Nelidesque Periclymenus, quem parva Methone / †felevis Elis equis et fluctibus obvius Aulon / caestibus adversos viderunt frangere vultus. — / Tu quoque Phrixeos remo, Poeantie, Colchos / bis Lemnon visure petis, nunc cuspide patris / inclitus, Herculeas olim moture sagittas.
reuse.text_english: Indeed, too, Tydeus rises from the Heraclean line, and the son of Neleus, Periclymenus, whom small Methone, Elis famed for its horses, and Aulon, facing the waves, saw breaking the faces of their opponents with fists. You too, Poeantius, seek Phrixian Colchis by oar, about to see Lemnos twice, now renowned for your father’s spear, once destined to wield Heraclean arrows.
